title: Section 5 (Lines 50–63)
subtitle: The flood spares their cottage, which becomes a golden temple

words.x: Completes the polysyndeton -que … -que … -que.

rows.en: Philemon reveals their joint decision to the gods:

notes.label: Emphatic Position
notes.body: Ovid opens this section with ambo (“both”) — and that is no accident. From the very start he stresses that these two act as a single unit. They obey, climb and respond together, and this word sets up the theme of unity for the whole passage.
notes.exam: In an exam: “Ovid places ambo (“both”) prominently at the start, establishing from the outset that Baucis and Philemon function as a unit. Their shared obedience to the gods foreshadows their later joint wish.”

notes.label: Historic Present
notes.body: This is the historic present — Ovid switches from past tense to present to make the action vivid. Instead of “they struggled” he gives us “they strive”, putting us right beside the couple as they labour up the hill.
notes.exam: In an exam: “Ovid uses the historic present nītuntur (“they strive”) to bring the reader into the moment. The switch from past narrative to present tense creates immediacy, making us feel the couple’s exertion as they climb.”

notes.label: Epic Simile
notes.quote: quantum semel īre sagitta missa potest
notes.trans: as far as an arrow, once shot, can go
notes.body: Ovid borrows from the epic poets here. Measuring a distance by how far an arrow flies is very Homeric and Virgilian — grand imagery you would expect for heroes, not elderly peasants. That is the point: he gives this humble couple the epic treatment.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The simile quantum semel īre sagitta missa potest (“as far as an arrow, once shot, can go”) lends epic grandeur to the scene. Ovid borrows the elevated register of Virgilian epic to underscore the divine significance of the moment.”

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: Enjambment is when a phrase runs over a line break. Here sagitta (“arrow”) sits at the end of one line and missa (“shot”) opens the next, so the sense literally flies across the gap — just as the arrow does through the air.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The enjambment of sagitta (“arrow”) at the line’s end, with missa (“discharged”) following, enacts the arrow’s trajectory. The reader must continue across the line break, just as the arrow travels through space.”

notes.label: Divine Favour
notes.body: Everyone else’s home is underwater, but their house is still standing. Ovid emphasises sua (“their own”) and tantum (“only”) to drive home how exceptional this is. The gods have singled these two out personally.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The juxtaposition of cētera (“the rest”) submerged by the marsh with sua tēcta manēre (“their own house remaining”) starkly demonstrates divine reward. The possessive sua (“their own”) emphasises that this salvation is personal and earned.”

notes.label: Anaphora
notes.trans: while they marvel… while they weep
notes.body: Anaphora is the repetition of a word at the start of clauses — here dum (“while”). The effect is to show two emotions happening at once: they are amazed at being saved and weeping for their lost neighbours. The structure captures that mixed feeling.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The anaphora of dum (“while”) creates a parallel between mīrantur (“they marvel”) and dēflent (“they weep”), showing Baucis and Philemon experiencing wonder and grief simultaneously. Their compassion for others, even in their own miraculous salvation, further demonstrates their moral worth.”

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.trans: that old, small house… is turned
notes.body: Hyperbaton means placing words in an unusual order — here Ovid makes us wait for the main verb. We hear “that old house, small even for its two owners” and keep wondering “yes, and?” Then finally: “is turned into a temple.” The delay builds suspense and makes the transformation land harder.
notes.exam: In an exam: “Ovid uses hyperbaton to delay the main verb vertitur (“is turned”), forcing the reader to dwell on the humble origins of the house in illa vetus casa parva (“that old, small house”). This creates anticipation and emphasises the contrast between poverty and divine splendour.”

notes.label: Historic Present
notes.trans: is turned… replaced… become yellow… are seen
notes.body: The historic present again — but now in a cluster. “Is turned… replace… turn golden… are seen.” Ovid fires off present-tense verbs one after another so we experience the metamorphosis in real time, happening before our eyes.
notes.exam: In an exam: “Ovid employs a series of historic presents — vertitur (“is turned”), subiēre (“replaced”), flāvēscunt (“become yellow”) — to make the transformation unfold in real time. The reader witnesses each miraculous change as it happens.”

notes.label: Polysyndeton
notes.body: Polysyndeton means piling up conjunctions — “and… and… and…”. The repeated -que makes the list feel breathless and overwhelming. Golden roof and carved doors and marble floor — too much to take in, just as Baucis and Philemon must have felt.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The polysyndeton in aurātaque… caelātaeque… adopertaque (“and golden… and engraved… and covered”) creates a sense of wonder and overwhelm, mirroring how Baucis and Philemon would have experienced the rapid succession of miracles. The repeated -que (“and”) suggests the changes are too numerous to fully process.”

notes.label: Characterising Diction
notes.body: Jupiter has just wiped out an entire village. Now he speaks “with a calm expression” — not worried, not guilty, simply calm. That contrast is chilling, exposing the vast gap between gods and mortals: what devastates humans costs Jupiter nothing.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The phrase placidō ōre (“with a calm expression”) characterises Jupiter as serenely in control. Having just destroyed an entire community, his untroubled demeanour underscores the vast gulf between divine and mortal experience.”

notes.label: Polyptoton
notes.body: Polyptoton is the repetition of the same word in different grammatical forms. Here Jupiter calls Philemon “honest” (iūste) and says he has an “honest” (iūstō) wife. The repetition hammers home the message: your justice is exactly why you have been saved.
notes.exam: In an exam: “The polyptoton iūste… iūstō (“honest… honest”) emphasises that justice is the couple’s defining characteristic. Jupiter’s repetition makes clear that their survival is not arbitrary but earned through moral integrity.”

notes.label: Framing
notes.body: Remember ambo (“both”) at the start? Now we get commūne (“shared”) at the end. Ovid frames the passage with words about togetherness. Even when making the biggest decision of their lives, they make it jointly — the whole point of their story.
notes.exam: In an exam: “Ovid’s use of commūne (“joint”) for their decision reinforces the theme of marital unity. Just as they opened the passage acting together (ambo), they close it making a shared choice, demonstrating that their bond defines every aspect of their lives.”
